# Editing an Icelandic machine translation of a chemistry textbook (fable-editor, version 1)

You are editing the Icelandic machine translation of an English chemistry textbook (OpenStax _Chemistry 2e_),
which is being published as a free textbook for Icelandic upper-secondary students (aged about 16 to 20).
Work as an experienced Icelandic editor (yfirlesari) with a good knowledge of chemistry.

The goal is text a student can learn from: correct Icelandic in a register that is semi-academic but fluent
for younger readers. Judge grammar, agreement, word order and word choice in context, sentence by sentence and
across the passage. The translation must stay faithful to the English: do not add, drop or localize content
(units, examples and names stay as in the English), and do not explain more than the English does.

## What you receive

One JSON document (`"format": "fable-editor-user/1"`):

- `chapter` and `module`: where the text comes from.
- `englishContext`: the whole module in English, for context. Read it to understand the passage; edit only
  the `segments`.
- `terms`: the project's house terminology for this text. Each entry has the English forms (`en`) and the
  ruled Icelandic (`is`); `avoid` lists renderings known to be wrong for it. Use the ruled term, inflected as
  the sentence needs, wherever the English uses that term in that sense. Where no ruled term applies, choose
  the established Icelandic chemistry term.
- `segments`: in document order, each with a `key`, the English (`en`) and the machine translation (`is`).
  Segments are sentences, paragraphs, captions, list items, table cells or titles.

Both texts hold inline markers in double square brackets, such as `[[term:millikrafta|term-00001]]`,
`[[i:aq]]`, `[[sub:2]]`, `[[MATH:3]]`, `[[xref:CNX_Chem_10_01_KMTPhases1]]` or
`[[link:gagnvirku hermun|http://openstax.org/l/16phetvisual]]`. They carry formatting, formulas and
references. Keep every marker, with the same type and the same number of markers in the segment. You may edit
the Icelandic words inside a `term`, `link`, `i`, `b`, `em` or `u` marker, but never the part after `|`, and
never the contents of `MATH`, `MEDIA`, `TABLE`, `xref` or `docref` markers, or of `sub` and `sup` markers that
hold formula parts. You may move a marker within the segment when Icelandic word order needs it.

## What to return

Only the segments you change, each with its `key`, the whole edited Icelandic text of that segment, and one or
more tags saying what kind of change you made:

- `terminology`: a term changed to the house term or the established term;
- `grammar`: inflection, agreement, case, or another grammatical error;
- `fluency`: word order, phrasing or idiom, so the sentence reads as natural Icelandic;
- `meaning`: the translation said something the English does not;
- `register`: too formal, too colloquial, or too hard for the readers;
- `punctuation`: punctuation, capitals, spacing or number format.

Leave a segment out when it is already good. Each key appears at most once. Change only what improves the
text; a good machine-translated sentence does not need rewording.

Coordination Chemistry of Transition Metals

We have daily contact with many transition metals. Iron occurs everywhere—from the rings in your spiral notebook and the cutlery in your kitchen to automobiles, ships, buildings, and in the hemoglobin in your blood. Titanium is useful in the manufacture of lightweight, durable products such as bicycle frames, artificial hips, and jewelry. Chromium is useful as a protective plating on plumbing fixtures and automotive detailing.

In addition to being used in their pure elemental forms, many compounds containing transition metals have numerous other applications. Silver nitrate is used to create mirrors, zirconium silicate provides friction in automotive brakes, and many important cancer-fighting agents, like the drug cisplatin and related species, are platinum compounds.

The variety of properties exhibited by transition metals is due to their complex valence shells. Unlike most main group metals where one oxidation state is normally observed, the valence shell structure of transition metals means that they usually occur in several different stable oxidation states. Transition metals are defined as those elements that have (or readily form) partially filled [[i:d]] orbitals. As shown in [[xref:CNX_Chem_19_01_PeriodicEConfig]], the [[term:[[i:d]]-block elements|term-00001]] in groups 3–11 are transition elements. The [[i:d]] orbitals fill with the copper family (group 11); for this reason, the next family (group 12) are technically not transition elements. However, the group 12 elements do display some of the same chemical properties and are commonly included in discussions of transition metals. Some chemists do treat the group 12 elements as transition metals.

The [[i:d]]-block elements are divided into the [[term:first transition series|term-00003]] (the elements Sc through Cu), the [[term:second transition series|term-00004]] (the elements Y through Ag), and the [[term:third transition series|term-00005]] (the element La and the elements Hf through Au). Actinium, Ac, is the first member of the [[term:fourth transition series|term-00006]], which also includes Rf through Rg.

The [[i:f]]-block elements are the elements Ce through Lu, which constitute the [[term:lanthanide series|term-00007]] (or [[term:lanthanoid series|term-00008]]), and the elements Th through Lr, which constitute the [[term:actinide series|term-00009]] (or [[term:actinoid series|term-00010]]). Because lanthanum behaves very much like the lanthanide elements, it is considered a lanthanide element, even though its electron configuration makes it the first member of the third transition series. Similarly, the behavior of actinium means it is part of the actinide series, although its electron configuration makes it the first member of the fourth transition series.

Valence Electrons in Transition Metals

Review how to write electron configurations, covered in the chapter on electronic structure and periodic properties of elements. Recall that for the transition and inner transition metals, it is necessary to remove the [[i:s]] electrons before the [[i:d]] or [[i:f]] electrons. Then, for each ion, give the electron configuration:

(a) cerium(III)

(b) lead(II)

(c) Ti[[sup:2+]]

(d) Am[[sup:3+]]

(e) Pd[[sup:2+]]

For the examples that are transition metals, determine to which series they belong.

Solution

For ions, the [[i:s]]-valence electrons are lost prior to the [[i:d]] or [[i:f]] electrons.

(a) Ce[[sup:3+]][Xe]4[[i:f]][[sup:1]]; Ce[[sup:3+]] is an inner transition element in the lanthanide series.

(b) Pb[[sup:2+]][Xe]6[[i:s]][[sup:2]]5[[i:d]][[sup:10]]4[[i:f]][[sup:14]]; the electrons are lost from the [[i:p]] orbital. This is a main group element.[[BR]](c) titanium(II) [Ar]3[[i:d]][[sup:2]]; first transition series

(d) americium(III) [Rn]5[[i:f]][[sup:6]]; actinide

(e) palladium(II) [Kr]4[[i:d]][[sup:8]]; second transition series

Check Your Learning

Give an example of an ion from the first transition series with no [[i:d]] electrons.

V[[sup:5+]] is one possibility. Other examples include Sc[[sup:3+]], Ti[[sup:4+]], Cr[[sup:6+]], and Mn[[sup:7+]].

Answer:

Uses of Lanthanides in Devices

Lanthanides (elements 57–71) are fairly abundant in the earth’s crust, despite their historic characterization as [[term:rare earth elements|term-00011]]. Thulium, the rarest naturally occurring lanthanoid, is more common in the earth’s crust than silver (4.5 [[MATH:1]] 10[[sup:−5]]% versus 0.79 [[MATH:2]] 10[[sup:−5]]% by mass). There are 17 rare earth elements, consisting of the 15 lanthanoids plus scandium and yttrium. They are called rare because they were once difficult to extract economically, so it was rare to have a pure sample; due to similar chemical properties, it is difficult to separate any one lanthanide from the others. However, newer separation methods, such as ion exchange resins similar to those found in home water softeners, make the separation of these elements easier and more economical. Most ores that contain these elements have low concentrations of all the rare earth elements mixed together.

The commercial applications of lanthanides are growing rapidly. For example, europium is important in flat screen displays found in computer monitors, cell phones, and televisions. Neodymium is useful in laptop hard drives and in the processes that convert crude oil into gasoline ([[xref:CNX_Chem_19_01_Lanthanoid]]). Holmium is found in dental and medical equipment. In addition, many alternative energy technologies rely heavily on lanthanoids. Neodymium and dysprosium are key components of hybrid vehicle engines and the magnets used in wind turbines.

As the demand for lanthanide materials has increased faster than supply, prices have also increased. In 2008, dysprosium cost $110/kg; by 2014, the price had increased to $470/kg. Increasing the supply of lanthanoid elements is one of the most significant challenges facing the industries that rely on the optical and magnetic properties of these materials.

The transition elements have many properties in common with other metals. They are almost all hard, high-melting solids that conduct heat and electricity well. They readily form alloys and lose electrons to form stable cations. In addition, transition metals form a wide variety of stable [[term:coordination compounds|term-00012]], in which the central metal atom or ion acts as a Lewis acid and accepts one or more pairs of electrons. Many different molecules and ions can donate lone pairs to the metal center, serving as Lewis bases. In this chapter, we shall focus primarily on the chemical behavior of the elements of the first transition series.

Properties of the Transition Elements

Transition metals demonstrate a wide range of chemical behaviors. As can be seen from their reduction potentials (see [[docref:Appendix H|m68866]]), some transition metals are strong reducing agents, whereas others have very low reactivity. For example, the lanthanides all form stable 3+ aqueous cations. The driving force for such oxidations is similar to that of alkaline earth metals such as Be or Mg, forming Be[[sup:2+]] and Mg[[sup:2+]]. On the other hand, materials like platinum and gold have much higher reduction potentials. Their ability to resist oxidation makes them useful materials for constructing circuits and jewelry.

Ions of the lighter [[i:d]]-block elements, such as Cr[[sup:3+]], Fe[[sup:3+]], and Co[[sup:2+]], form colorful hydrated ions that are stable in water. However, ions in the period just below these (Mo[[sup:3+]], Ru[[sup:3+]], and Ir[[sup:2+]]) are unstable and react readily with oxygen from the air. The majority of simple, water-stable ions formed by the heavier [[i:d]]-block elements are oxyanions such as [[MATH:3]] and [[MATH:4]]

Ruthenium, osmium, rhodium, iridium, palladium, and platinum are the [[term:platinum metals|term-00013]]. With difficulty, they form simple cations that are stable in water, and, unlike the earlier elements in the second and third transition series, they do not form stable oxyanions.

Both the [[i:d]]- and [[i:f]]-block elements react with nonmetals to form binary compounds; heating is often required. These elements react with halogens to form a variety of halides ranging in oxidation state from 1+ to 6+. On heating, oxygen reacts with all of the transition elements except palladium, platinum, silver, and gold. The oxides of these latter metals can be formed using other reactants, but they decompose upon heating. The [[i:f]]-block elements, the elements of group 3, and the elements of the first transition series except copper react with aqueous solutions of acids, forming hydrogen gas and solutions of the corresponding salts.

Transition metals can form compounds with a wide range of oxidation states. Some of the observed oxidation states of the elements of the first transition series are shown in [[xref:CNX_Chem_19_01_Oxistatra]]. As we move from left to right across the first transition series, we see that the number of common oxidation states increases at first to a maximum towards the middle of the table, then decreases. The values in the table are typical values; there are other known values, and it is possible to synthesize new additions. For example, in 2014, researchers were successful in synthesizing a new oxidation state of iridium (9+).

For the elements scandium through manganese (the first half of the first transition series), the highest oxidation state corresponds to the loss of all of the electrons in both the [[i:s]] and [[i:d]] orbitals of their valence shells. The titanium(IV) ion, for example, is formed when the titanium atom loses its two 3[[i:d]] and two 4[[i:s]] electrons. These highest oxidation states are the most stable forms of scandium, titanium, and vanadium. However, it is not possible to continue to remove all of the valence electrons from metals as we continue through the series. Iron is known to form oxidation states from 2+ to 6+, with iron(II) and iron(III) being the most common. Most of the elements of the first transition series form ions with a charge of 2+ or 3+ that are stable in water, although those of the early members of the series can be readily oxidized by air.

The elements of the second and third transition series generally are more stable in higher oxidation states than are the elements of the first series. In general, the atomic radius increases down a group, which leads to the ions of the second and third series being larger than are those in the first series. Removing electrons from orbitals that are located farther from the nucleus is easier than removing electrons close to the nucleus. For example, molybdenum and tungsten, members of group 6, are limited mostly to an oxidation state of 6+ in aqueous solution. Chromium, the lightest member of the group, forms stable Cr[[sup:3+]] ions in water and, in the absence of air, less stable Cr[[sup:2+]] ions. The sulfide with the highest oxidation state for chromium is Cr[[sub:2]]S[[sub:3]], which contains the Cr[[sup:3+]] ion. Molybdenum and tungsten form sulfides in which the metals exhibit oxidation states of 4+ and 6+.

Preparation of the Transition Elements

Ancient civilizations knew about iron, copper, silver, and gold. The time periods in human history known as the Bronze Age and Iron Age mark the advancements in which societies learned to isolate certain metals and use them to make tools and goods. Naturally occurring ores of copper, silver, and gold can contain high concentrations of these metals in elemental form ([[xref:CNX_Chem_19_01_CuFeAu]]). Iron, on the other hand, occurs on earth almost exclusively in oxidized forms, such as rust (Fe[[sub:2]]O[[sub:3]]). The earliest known iron implements were made from iron meteorites. Surviving iron artifacts dating from approximately 4000 to 2500 BC are rare, but all known examples contain specific alloys of iron and nickel that occur only in extraterrestrial objects, not on earth. It took thousands of years of technological advances before civilizations developed iron [[term:smelting|term-00014]], the ability to extract a pure element from its naturally occurring ores and for iron tools to become common.

Transition metals occur in nature in various forms. Examples include (a) a nugget of copper, (b) a deposit of gold, and (c) an ore containing oxidized iron. Generally, the transition elements are extracted from minerals found in a variety of ores. However, the ease of their recovery varies widely, depending on the concentration of the element in the ore, the identity of the other elements present, and the difficulty of reducing the element to the free metal.

In general, it is not difficult to reduce ions of the [[i:d]]-block elements to the free element. Carbon is a sufficiently strong reducing agent in most cases. However, like the ions of the more active main group metals, ions of the [[i:f]]-block elements must be isolated by electrolysis or by reduction with an active metal such as calcium.

We shall discuss the processes used for the isolation of iron, copper, and silver because these three processes illustrate the principal means of isolating most of the [[i:d]]-block metals. In general, each of these processes involves three principal steps: preliminary treatment, smelting, and refining.

Preliminary treatment. In general, there is an initial treatment of the ores to make them suitable for the extraction of the metals. This usually involves crushing or grinding the ore, concentrating the metal-bearing components, and sometimes treating these substances chemically to convert them into compounds that are easier to reduce to the metal.

Smelting. The next step is the extraction of the metal in the molten state, a process called smelting, which includes reduction of the metallic compound to the metal. Impurities may be removed by the addition of a compound that forms a slag—a substance with a low melting point that can be readily separated from the molten metal.

Refining. The final step in the recovery of a metal is refining the metal. Low boiling metals such as zinc and mercury can be refined by distillation. When fused on an inclined table, low melting metals like tin flow away from higher-melting impurities. Electrolysis is another common method for refining metals.

Isolation of Iron

The early application of iron to the manufacture of tools and weapons was possible because of the wide distribution of iron ores and the ease with which iron compounds in the ores could be reduced by carbon. For a long time, charcoal was the form of carbon used in the reduction process. The production and use of iron became much more widespread about 1620, when coke was introduced as the reducing agent. Coke is a form of carbon formed by heating coal in the absence of air to remove impurities.

The first step in the metallurgy of iron is usually roasting the ore (heating the ore in air) to remove water, decomposing carbonates into oxides, and converting sulfides into oxides. The oxides are then reduced in a blast furnace that is 80–100 feet high and about 25 feet in diameter ([[xref:CNX_Chem_19_01_BlastFurn]]) in which the roasted ore, coke, and limestone (impure CaCO[[sub:3]]) are introduced continuously into the top. Molten iron and slag are withdrawn at the bottom. The entire stock in a furnace may weigh several hundred tons.

Within a blast furnace, different reactions occur in different temperature zones. Carbon monoxide is generated in the hotter bottom regions and rises upward to reduce the iron oxides to pure iron through a series of reactions that take place in the upper regions.

Much of the iron produced is refined and converted into steel. [[term:Steel|term-00015]] is made from iron by removing impurities and adding substances such as manganese, chromium, nickel, tungsten, molybdenum, and vanadium to produce alloys with properties that make the material suitable for specific uses. Most steels also contain small but definite percentages of carbon (0.04%–2.5%). However, a large part of the carbon contained in iron must be removed in the manufacture of steel; otherwise, the excess carbon would make the iron brittle.

Isolation of Copper

The most important ores of copper contain copper sulfides (such as covellite, CuS), although copper oxides (such as tenorite, CuO) and copper hydroxycarbonates [such as malachite, Cu[[sub:2]](OH)[[sub:2]]CO[[sub:3]]] are sometimes found. In the production of copper metal, the concentrated sulfide ore is roasted to remove part of the sulfur as sulfur dioxide. The remaining mixture, which consists of Cu[[sub:2]]S, FeS, FeO, and SiO[[sub:2]], is mixed with limestone, which serves as a flux (a material that aids in the removal of impurities), and heated. Molten slag forms as the iron and silica are removed by Lewis acid-base reactions:

In these reactions, the silicon dioxide behaves as a Lewis acid, which accepts a pair of electrons from the Lewis base (the oxide ion).

Reduction of the Cu[[sub:2]]S that remains after smelting is accomplished by blowing air through the molten material. The air converts part of the Cu[[sub:2]]S into Cu[[sub:2]]O. As soon as copper(I) oxide is formed, it is reduced by the remaining copper(I) sulfide to metallic copper:

The copper obtained in this way is called blister copper because of its characteristic appearance, which is due to the air blisters it contains ([[xref:CNX_Chem_19_01_BlisterCu]]). This impure copper is cast into large plates, which are used as anodes in the electrolytic refining of the metal (which is described in the chapter on electrochemistry).

Isolation of Silver

Silver sometimes occurs in large nuggets ([[xref:CNX_Chem_19_01_Ag]]) but more frequently in veins and related deposits. At one time, panning was an effective method of isolating both silver and gold nuggets. Due to their low reactivity, these metals, and a few others, occur in deposits as nuggets. The discovery of platinum was due to Spanish explorers in Central America mistaking platinum nuggets for silver. When the metal is not in the form of nuggets, it often useful to employ a process called [[term:hydrometallurgy|term-00016]] to separate silver from its ores. Hydrology involves the separation of a metal from a mixture by first converting it into soluble ions and then extracting and reducing them to precipitate the pure metal. In the presence of air, alkali metal cyanides readily form the soluble dicyanoargentate(I) ion, [[MATH:7]] from silver metal or silver-containing compounds such as Ag[[sub:2]]S and AgCl. Anhydrous halides of each of the transition elements can be prepared by the direct reaction of the metal with halogens. For example:

Heating a metal halide with additional metal can be used to form a halide of the metal with a lower oxidation state:

The stoichiometry of the metal halide that results from the reaction of the metal with a halogen is determined by the relative amounts of metal and halogen and by the strength of the halogen as an oxidizing agent. Generally, fluorine forms fluoride-containing metals in their highest oxidation states. The other halogens may not form analogous compounds.

In general, the preparation of stable water solutions of the halides of the metals of the first transition series is by the addition of a hydrohalic acid to carbonates, hydroxides, oxides, or other compounds that contain basic anions. Sample reactions are:

Most of the first transition series metals also dissolve in acids, forming a solution of the salt and hydrogen gas. For example:

The polarity of bonds with transition metals varies based not only upon the electronegativities of the atoms involved but also upon the oxidation state of the transition metal. Remember that bond polarity is a continuous spectrum with electrons being shared evenly (covalent bonds) at one extreme and electrons being transferred completely (ionic bonds) at the other. No bond is ever 100% ionic, and the degree to which the electrons are evenly distributed determines many properties of the compound. Transition metal halides with low oxidation numbers form more ionic bonds. For example, titanium(II) chloride and titanium(III) chloride (TiCl[[sub:2]] and TiCl[[sub:3]]) have high melting points that are characteristic of ionic compounds, but titanium(IV) chloride (TiCl[[sub:4]]) is a volatile liquid, consistent with having covalent titanium-chlorine bonds. All halides of the heavier [[i:d]]-block elements have significant covalent characteristics.

The covalent behavior of the transition metals with higher oxidation states is exemplified by the reaction of the metal tetrahalides with water. Like covalent silicon tetrachloride, both the titanium and vanadium tetrahalides react with water to give solutions containing the corresponding hydrohalic acids and the metal oxides:

Oxides

As with the halides, the nature of bonding in oxides of the transition elements is determined by the oxidation state of the metal. Oxides with low oxidation states tend to be more ionic, whereas those with higher oxidation states are more covalent. These variations in bonding are because the electronegativities of the elements are not fixed values. The electronegativity of an element increases with increasing oxidation state. Transition metals in low oxidation states have lower electronegativity values than oxygen; therefore, these metal oxides are ionic. Transition metals in very high oxidation states have electronegativity values close to that of oxygen, which leads to these oxides being covalent.

The oxides of the first transition series can be prepared by heating the metals in air. These oxides are Sc[[sub:2]]O[[sub:3]], TiO[[sub:2]], V[[sub:2]]O[[sub:5]], Cr[[sub:2]]O[[sub:3]], Mn[[sub:3]]O[[sub:4]], Fe[[sub:3]]O[[sub:4]], Co[[sub:3]]O[[sub:4]], NiO, and CuO.

Alternatively, these oxides and other oxides (with the metals in different oxidation states) can be produced by heating the corresponding hydroxides, carbonates, or oxalates in an inert atmosphere. Iron(II) oxide can be prepared by heating iron(II) oxalate, and cobalt(II) oxide is produced by heating cobalt(II) hydroxide:

With the exception of CrO[[sub:3]] and Mn[[sub:2]]O[[sub:7]], transition metal oxides are not soluble in water. They can react with acids and, in a few cases, with bases. Overall, oxides of transition metals with the lowest oxidation states are basic (and react with acids), the intermediate ones are amphoteric, and the highest oxidation states are primarily acidic. Basic metal oxides at a low oxidation state react with aqueous acids to form solutions of salts and water. Examples include the reaction of cobalt(II) oxide accepting protons from nitric acid, and scandium(III) oxide accepting protons from hydrochloric acid:

The oxides of metals with oxidation states of 4+ are amphoteric, and most are not soluble in either acids or bases. Vanadium(V) oxide, chromium(VI) oxide, and manganese(VII) oxide are acidic. They react with solutions of hydroxides to form salts of the oxyanions [[MATH:8]] [[MATH:9]] and [[MATH:10]] For example, the complete ionic equation for the reaction of chromium(VI) oxide with a strong base is given by:

Chromium(VI) oxide and manganese(VII) oxide react with water to form the acids H[[sub:2]]CrO[[sub:4]] and HMnO[[sub:4]], respectively.

Hydroxides

When a soluble hydroxide is added to an aqueous solution of a salt of a transition metal of the first transition series, a gelatinous precipitate forms. For example, adding a solution of sodium hydroxide to a solution of cobalt sulfate produces a gelatinous pink or blue precipitate of cobalt(II) hydroxide. The net ionic equation is:

In this and many other cases, these precipitates are hydroxides containing the transition metal ion, hydroxide ions, and water coordinated to the transition metal. In other cases, the precipitates are hydrated oxides composed of the metal ion, oxide ions, and water of hydration:

These substances do not contain hydroxide ions. However, both the hydroxides and the hydrated oxides react with acids to form salts and water. When precipitating a metal from solution, it is necessary to avoid an excess of hydroxide ion, as this may lead to complex ion formation as discussed later in this chapter. The precipitated metal hydroxides can be separated for further processing or for waste disposal.

Many of the elements of the first transition series form insoluble carbonates. It is possible to prepare these carbonates by the addition of a soluble carbonate salt to a solution of a transition metal salt. High Temperature Superconductors

A [[term:superconductor|term-00017]] is a substance that conducts electricity with no resistance. This lack of resistance means that there is no energy loss during the transmission of electricity. This would lead to a significant reduction in the cost of electricity.

Most currently used, commercial superconducting materials, such as NbTi and Nb[[sub:3]]Sn, do not become superconducting until they are cooled below 23 K (−250 °C). This requires the use of liquid helium, which has a boiling temperature of 4 K and is expensive and difficult to handle. The cost of liquid helium has deterred the widespread application of superconductors.

One of the most exciting scientific discoveries of the 1980s was the characterization of compounds that exhibit superconductivity at temperatures above 90 K. (Compared to liquid helium, 90 K is a high temperature.) Typical among the high-temperature superconducting materials are oxides containing yttrium (or one of several rare earth elements), barium, and copper in a 1:2:3 ratio. The formula of the ionic yttrium compound is YBa[[sub:2]]Cu[[sub:3]]O[[sub:7]].

The new materials become superconducting at temperatures close to 90 K ([[xref:CNX_Chem_19_01_ResTemp]]), temperatures that can be reached by cooling with liquid nitrogen (boiling temperature of 77 K). Not only are liquid nitrogen-cooled materials easier to handle, but the cooling costs are also about 1000 times lower than for liquid helium.

Further advances during the same period included materials that became superconducting at even higher temperatures and with a wider array of materials. The DuPont team led by Uma Chowdry and Arthur Sleight identified Bismouth-Strontium-Copper-Oxides that became superconducting at temperatures as high as 110 K and, importantly, did not contain rare earth elements. Advances continued through the subsequent decades until, in 2020, a team led by Ranga Dias at University of Rochester announced the development of a room-temperature superconductor, opening doors to widespread applications. More research and development is needed to realize the potential of these materials, but the possibilities are very promising.

Although the brittle, fragile nature of these materials presently hampers their commercial applications, they have tremendous potential that researchers are hard at work improving their processes to help realize. Superconducting transmission lines would carry current for hundreds of miles with no loss of power due to resistance in the wires. This could allow generating stations to be located in areas remote from population centers and near the natural resources necessary for power production. The first project demonstrating the viability of high-temperature superconductor power transmission was established in New York in 2008.

Researchers are also working on using this technology to develop other applications, such as smaller and more powerful microchips. In addition, high-temperature superconductors can be used to generate magnetic fields for applications such as medical devices, magnetic levitation trains, and containment fields for nuclear fusion reactors ([[xref:CNX_Chem_19_01_Maglevtrai]]).

The bonding in the simple compounds of the transition elements ranges from ionic to covalent. In their lower oxidation states, the transition elements form ionic compounds; in their higher oxidation states, they form covalent compounds or polyatomic ions. The variation in oxidation states exhibited by the transition elements gives these compounds a metal-based, oxidation-reduction chemistry. The chemistry of several classes of compounds containing elements of the transition series follows.

Key Concepts and Summary

The transition metals are elements with partially filled [[i:d]] orbitals, located in the [[i:d]]-block of the periodic table. The reactivity of the transition elements varies widely from very active metals such as scandium and iron to almost inert elements, such as the platinum metals. The type of chemistry used in the isolation of the elements from their ores depends upon the concentration of the element in its ore and the difficulty of reducing ions of the elements to the metals. Metals that are more active are more difficult to reduce.

Transition metals exhibit chemical behavior typical of metals. For example, they oxidize in air upon heating and react with elemental halogens to form halides. Those elements that lie above hydrogen in the activity series react with acids, producing salts and hydrogen gas. Oxides, hydroxides, and carbonates of transition metal compounds in low oxidation states are basic. Halides and other salts are generally stable in water, although oxygen must be excluded in some cases. Most transition metals form a variety of stable oxidation states, allowing them to demonstrate a wide range of chemical reactivity.

There are 17 rare earth elements, consisting of the 15 lanthanoids plus scandium and yttrium. However, newer separation methods, such as ion exchange resins similar to those found in home water softeners, make the separation of these elements easier and more economical. Túlíum, sjaldgæfasti náttúrulegi lantaníðinn, er algengari í jarðskorpunni en silfur (4,5 [[MATH:1]] 10[[sup:−5]]% á móti 0,79 [[MATH:2]] 10[[sup:−5]]% miðað við massa). Til eru 17 sjaldgæfir jarðmálmar, sem samanstanda af 15 lantaníðum auk skandíums og yttríums. Þeir eru kallaðir sjaldgæfir vegna þess að áður var erfitt að vinna þá á hagkvæman hátt, svo það var sjaldgæft að eiga hreint sýni; vegna svipaðra efnafræðilegra eiginleika er erfitt að aðskilja einn lantaníða frá öðrum. Nýrri aðskilnaðaraðferðir, svo sem jónaskiptakvoður svipaðar þeim sem finnast í vatnsmýkingartækjum fyrir heimili, gera aðskilnað þessara frumefna hins vegar auðveldari og hagkvæmari. Flestar málmgrýtisgerðir sem innihalda þessi frumefni hafa lágan styrk allra sjaldgæfu jarðmálmanna í bland."},{"key":"m68842:para:fs-idm256905072","en":"The commercial applications of lanthanides are growing rapidly. For example, europium is important in flat screen displays found in computer monitors, cell phones, and televisions. Neodymium is useful in laptop hard drives and in the processes that convert crude oil into gasoline ([[xref:CNX_Chem_19_01_Lanthanoid]]). Holmium is found in dental and medical equipment. In addition, many alternative energy technologies rely heavily on lanthanoids. Neodymium and dysprosium are key components of hybrid vehicle engines and the magnets used in wind turbines.","is":"Notkun lantaníða í atvinnuskyni fer ört vaxandi. Neódým er nytsamlegt í hörðum drifum fartölva og í ferlum sem breyta hráolíu í bensín ([[xref:CNX_Chem_19_01_Lanthanoid]]). Hólmíum er að finna í tannlækninga- og lækningatækjum. Auk þess byggir mörg önnur orkutækni mikið á lantaníðum. Neódým og dysprósíum eru lykilþættir í vélum tvinnbíla og seglum sem notaðir eru í vindmyllum."},{"key":"m68842:para:fs-idm272757680","en":"As the demand for lanthanide materials has increased faster than supply, prices have also increased. In 2008, dysprosium cost $110/kg; by 2014, the price had increased to $470/kg. Increasing the supply of lanthanoid elements is one of the most significant challenges facing the industries that rely on the optical and magnetic properties of these materials.","is":"Þar sem eftirspurn eftir lantaníðum hefur aukist hraðar en framboð hefur verð einnig hækkað. Þetta bogadregna form hefur þunna, oddmjóa framlengingu sem nær að yfirborði málmdisksins."},{"key":"m68842:para:fs-idm102288080","en":"The transition elements have many properties in common with other metals. They are almost all hard, high-melting solids that conduct heat and electricity well. They readily form alloys and lose electrons to form stable cations. In addition, transition metals form a wide variety of stable [[term:coordination compounds|term-00012]], in which the central metal atom or ion acts as a Lewis acid and accepts one or more pairs of electrons. Many different molecules and ions can donate lone pairs to the metal center, serving as Lewis bases. In this chapter, we shall focus primarily on the chemical behavior of the elements of the first transition series.","is":"Hliðarfrumefnin eiga marga eiginleika sameiginlega með öðrum málmum. Þau eru næstum öll hörð, hábræðsluföst efni sem leiða vel hita og rafmagn. Þau mynda auðveldlega málmblöndur og tapa rafeindum til að mynda stöðugar katjónir. Auk þess mynda hliðarmálmar fjölbreytt úrval stöðugra [[term:girðisambanda|term-00012]], þar sem miðjumálmatómið eða jónin virkar sem Lewis-sýra og tekur við einu eða fleiri rafeindapörum. Margar mismunandi sameindir og jónir geta gefið stök rafeindapör til málmmiðjunnar og virka þannig sem Lewis-basar. Í þessum kafla munum við aðallega einbeita okkur að efnafræðilegri hegðun frumefna fyrstu hliðarfrumefnaraðarinnar."},{"key":"m68842:title:fs-idm66147136-title","en":"Properties of the Transition Elements","is":"Eiginleikar hliðarfrumefna"},{"key":"m68842:para:fs-idm265281664","en":"Transition metals demonstrate a wide range of chemical behaviors. As can be seen from their reduction potentials (see [[docref:Appendix H|m68866]]), some transition metals are strong reducing agents, whereas others have very low reactivity. For example, the lanthanides all form stable 3+ aqueous cations. The driving force for such oxidations is similar to that of alkaline earth metals such as Be or Mg, forming Be[[sup:2+]] and Mg[[sup:2+]]. On the other hand, materials like platinum and gold have much higher reduction potentials. Their ability to resist oxidation makes them useful materials for constructing circuits and jewelry.","is":"Hliðarmálmar sýna fjölbreytta efnafræðilega hegðun. Eins og sjá má af afoxunarmætti þeirra (sjá [[docref:viðauka H|m68866]]), eru sumir hliðarmálmar sterkir afoxarar, á meðan aðrir hafa mjög lítinn hvarfgirni. Til dæmis mynda öll lantaníð stöðugar 3+ vatnskatjónir. Drifkrafturinn fyrir slíkum oxunum er svipaður og hjá jarðalkalímálmum eins og Be eða Mg, sem mynda Be[[sup:2+]] og Mg[[sup:2+]]. Á hinn bóginn hafa efni eins og platína og gull mun hærri afoxunarmátt. Hæfni þeirra til að standast oxun gerir þau að nytsamlegum efnum til að smíða rafrásir og skartgripi."},{"key":"m68842:para:fs-idm124317440","en":"Ions of the lighter [[i:d]]-block elements, such as Cr[[sup:3+]], Fe[[sup:3+]], and Co[[sup:2+]], form colorful hydrated ions that are stable in water. However, ions in the period just below these (Mo[[sup:3+]], Ru[[sup:3+]], and Ir[[sup:2+]]) are unstable and react readily with oxygen from the air. The majority of simple, water-stable ions formed by the heavier [[i:d]]-block elements are oxyanions such as [[MATH:3]] and [[MATH:4]]","is":"Jónir léttari [[i:d]]-sviðs frumefna, eins og Cr[[sup:3+]], Fe[[sup:3+]] og Co[[sup:2+]], mynda litríkar vökvaðar jónir sem eru stöðugar í vatni. Hins vegar eru jónir í lotunni rétt fyrir neðan þessar (Mo[[sup:3+]], Ru[[sup:3+]] og Ir[[sup:2+]]) óstöðugar og hvarfast auðveldlega við súrefni úr loftinu. Meirihluti einfaldra, vatnsstöðugra jóna sem myndast af þyngri [[i:d]]-sviðs frumefnum eru oxíðanjónir eins og [[MATH:3]] og [[MATH:4]]"},{"key":"m68842:para:fs-idm66167072","en":"Ruthenium, osmium, rhodium, iridium, palladium, and platinum are the [[term:platinum metals|term-00013]]. With difficulty, they form simple cations that are stable in water, and, unlike the earlier elements in the second and third transition series, they do not form stable oxyanions.","is":"Rúþen, osmíum, ródíum, iridíum, palladíum og platína eru [[term:platínumálmarnir|term-00013]]. Með erfiðismunum mynda þeir einfaldar katjónir sem eru stöðugar í vatni og, ólíkt fyrri frumefnum í annarri og þriðju hliðarfrumefnaröðinni, mynda þeir ekki stöðugar oxíðanjónir."},{"key":"m68842:para:fs-idm273645328","en":"Both the [[i:d]]- and [[i:f]]-block elements react with nonmetals to form binary compounds; heating is often required. These elements react with halogens to form a variety of halides ranging in oxidation state from 1+ to 6+. On heating, oxygen reacts with all of the transition elements except palladium, platinum, silver, and gold. The oxides of these latter metals can be formed using other reactants, but they decompose upon heating. The [[i:f]]-block elements, the elements of group 3, and the elements of the first transition series except copper react with aqueous solutions of acids, forming hydrogen gas and solutions of the corresponding salts.","is":"Bæði [[i:d]]- og [[i:f]]-sviðs frumefni hvarfast við málmleysingja til að mynda tvíundarsambönd; oft er þörf á hitun. Þessi frumefni hvarfast við halógena til að mynda margs konar halíð með oxunartölur frá 1+ til 6+. Við hitun hvarfast súrefni við öll hliðarfrumefnin nema palladíum, platínu, silfur og gull. Oxíð þessara síðarnefndu málma er hægt að mynda með öðrum hvarfefnum, en þau brotna niður við hitun. [[i:f]]-sviðs frumefnin, frumefni 3. flokks og frumefni fyrstu hliðarfrumefnaraðarinnar nema kopar hvarfast við vatnslausnir sýra og mynda vetnisgas og lausnir samsvarandi salta."},{"key":"m68842:para:fs-idm34798016","en":"Transition metals can form compounds with a wide range of oxidation states. Some of the observed oxidation states of the elements of the first transition series are shown in [[xref:CNX_Chem_19_01_Oxistatra]]. As we move from left to right across the first transition series, we see that the number of common oxidation states increases at first to a maximum towards the middle of the table, then decreases. The values in the table are typical values; there are other known values, and it is possible to synthesize new additions. For example, in 2014, researchers were successful in synthesizing a new oxidation state of iridium (9+).","is":"Hliðarmálmar geta myndað efnasambönd með fjölbreyttar oxunartölur. Sumar af þeim oxunartölum sem sjást hjá frumefnum fyrstu hliðarfrumefnaraðarinnar eru sýndar í [[xref:CNX_Chem_19_01_Oxistatra]]. Þegar við færum okkur frá vinstri til hægri yfir fyrstu hliðarfrumefnaröðina sjáum við að fjöldi algengra oxunartalna eykst í fyrstu að hámarki í miðri töflunni, en fækkar síðan. Gildin í töflunni eru dæmigerð gildi; önnur þekkt gildi eru til og hægt er að búa til nýjar viðbætur. Til dæmis tókst vísindamönnum árið 2014 að búa til nýja oxunartölu iridíums (9+)."},{"key":"m68842:caption:CNX_Chem_19_01_Oxistatra-caption","en":"Transition metals of the first transition series can form compounds with varying oxidation states.","is":"Hliðarmálmar fyrstu hliðarfrumefnaraðarinnar geta myndað efnasambönd með mismunandi oxunartölur."},{"key":"m68842:alt:fs-idm178431040-alt","en":"A table is shown with 10 columns and 8 rows. Áttunda röðin sýnir gildið 7 plús undir Mn."},{"key":"m68842:para:fs-idm168637008","en":"For the elements scandium through manganese (the first half of the first transition series), the highest oxidation state corresponds to the loss of all of the electrons in both the [[i:s]] and [[i:d]] orbitals of their valence shells. The titanium(IV) ion, for example, is formed when the titanium atom loses its two 3[[i:d]] and two 4[[i:s]] electrons. These highest oxidation states are the most stable forms of scandium, titanium, and vanadium. However, it is not possible to continue to remove all of the valence electrons from metals as we continue through the series. Iron is known to form oxidation states from 2+ to 6+, with iron(II) and iron(III) being the most common. Most of the elements of the first transition series form ions with a charge of 2+ or 3+ that are stable in water, although those of the early members of the series can be readily oxidized by air.","is":"Fyrir frumefnin skandín til mangan (fyrri helmingur fyrstu hliðarfrumefnaraðarinnar) samsvarar hæsta oxunarástandið því að missa allar rafeindirnar í bæði [[i:s]]- og [[i:d]]-svigrúmum gildisskeljar þeirra. Títan(IV)-jónin myndast til dæmis þegar títanatóm missir tvær 3[[i:d]]- og tvær 4[[i:s]]-rafeindir sínar. Þessi hæstu oxunarástönd eru stöðugustu form skandíns, títans og vanadíns. Hins vegar er ekki hægt að halda áfram að fjarlægja allar gildisrafeindir úr málmum eftir því sem við förum lengra í röðinni. Vitað er að járn myndar oxunarástönd frá 2+ til 6+, þar sem járn(II) og járn(III) eru algengust. Flest frumefni fyrstu hliðarfrumefnaraðarinnar mynda jónir með hleðsluna 2+ eða 3+ sem eru stöðugar í vatni, þótt auðvelt sé að oxa jónir fyrstu frumefnanna í röðinni með lofti."},{"key":"m68842:para:fs-idm217974912","en":"The elements of the second and third transition series generally are more stable in higher oxidation states than are the elements of the first series. In general, the atomic radius increases down a group, which leads to the ions of the second and third series being larger than are those in the first series. Removing electrons from orbitals that are located farther from the nucleus is easier than removing electrons close to the nucleus. For example, molybdenum and tungsten, members of group 6, are limited mostly to an oxidation state of 6+ in aqueous solution. Chromium, the lightest member of the group, forms stable Cr[[sup:3+]] ions in water and, in the absence of air, less stable Cr[[sup:2+]] ions. The sulfide with the highest oxidation state for chromium is Cr[[sub:2]]S[[sub:3]], which contains the Cr[[sup:3+]] ion. Molybdenum and tungsten form sulfides in which the metals exhibit oxidation states of 4+ and 6+.","is":"Frumefni annarrar og þriðju hliðarfrumefnaraðarinnar eru almennt stöðugri í hærri oxunarástöndum en frumefni fyrstu raðarinnar. Almennt eykst atómradíus niður eftir flokki, sem leiðir til þess að jónir annarrar og þriðju raðarinnar eru stærri en þær í fyrstu röðinni. Auðveldara er að fjarlægja rafeindir úr svigrúmum sem eru lengra frá kjarnanum en að fjarlægja rafeindir nálægt kjarnanum. Til dæmis eru mólýbden og volfram, sem eru í flokki 6, að mestu takmörkuð við oxunarástandið 6+ í vatnslausn. Króm, léttasta frumefnið í flokknum, myndar stöðugar Cr[[sup:3+]]-jónir í vatni og, í fjarveru lofts, óstöðugri Cr[[sup:2+]]-jónir. Súlfíðið með hæsta oxunarástand króms er Cr[[sub:2]]S[[sub:3]], sem inniheldur Cr[[sup:3+]]-jónina. Mólýbden og volfram mynda súlfíð þar sem málmarnir sýna oxunarástöndin 4+ og 6+."},{"key":"m68842:example-title:fs-idm126999824-title","en":"Activity of the Transition Metals","is":"Virkni hliðarfrumefna"},{"key":"m68842:para:fs-idm43231280","en":"Which is the strongest oxidizing agent in acidic solution: dichromate ion, which contains chromium(VI), permanganate ion, which contains manganese(VII), or titanium dioxide, which contains titanium(IV)?","is":"Hvert er sterkasta oxunarefnið í súrri lausn: díkrómatjón, sem inniheldur króm(VI), permanganatjón, sem inniheldur mangan(VII), eða títantvíoxíð, sem inniheldur títan(IV)?"},{"key":"m68842:para-title:fs-idm124155920-title","en":"Solution","is":"Lausn"},{"key":"m68842:para:fs-idm124155920","en":"First, we need to look up the reduction half reactions (in [[docref:Appendix L|m68870]]) for each oxide in the specified oxidation state:","is":"Fyrst þurfum við að fletta upp afoxunarhvarfhelmingunum (í [[docref:viðauka L|m68870]]) fyrir hvert oxíð í tilgreindu oxunarástandi:"},{"key":"m68842:para:fs-idm158628640","en":"A larger reduction potential means that it is easier to reduce the reactant. Permanganate, with the largest reduction potential, is the strongest oxidizer under these conditions. Dichromate is next, followed by titanium dioxide as the weakest oxidizing agent (the hardest to reduce) of this set.","is":"Stærri afoxunarmættispenna þýðir að auðveldara er að afoxa hvarfefnið. Permanganat, með stærstu afoxunarmættispennuna, er sterkasti oxarinn við þessar aðstæður. Næst kemur díkrómat og síðan títantvíoxíð sem veikasta oxunarefnið (það sem er erfiðast að afoxa) í þessu setti."},{"key":"m68842:para-title:fs-idm193921504-title","en":"Check Your Learning","is":"Skoðaðu þekkingu þína"},{"key":"m68842:para:fs-idm193921504","en":"Predict what reaction (if any) will occur between HCl and Co([[i:s]]), and between HBr and Pt([[i:s]]). Þú þarft að nota staðlaðar afoxunarmættispennur úr [[docref:viðauka L|m68870]]."},{"key":"m68842:para:fs-idm178358032","en":"[[MATH:5]] no reaction because Pt([[i:s]]) will not be oxidized by H[[sup:+]]","is":"[[MATH:5]] ekkert hvarf því Pt([[i:s]]) verður ekki oxað af H[[sup:+]]"},{"key":"m68842:note-title:fs-idm123798544-title","en":"Answer:","is":"Svar:"},{"key":"m68842:title:fs-idm197634688-title","en":"Preparation of the Transition Elements","is":"Framleiðsla hliðarfrumefna"},{"key":"m68842:para:fs-idm265294720","en":"Ancient civilizations knew about iron, copper, silver, and gold. The time periods in human history known as the Bronze Age and Iron Age mark the advancements in which societies learned to isolate certain metals and use them to make tools and goods. Naturally occurring ores of copper, silver, and gold can contain high concentrations of these metals in elemental form ([[xref:CNX_Chem_19_01_CuFeAu]]). Iron, on the other hand, occurs on earth almost exclusively in oxidized forms, such as rust (Fe[[sub:2]]O[[sub:3]]). The earliest known iron implements were made from iron meteorites. Surviving iron artifacts dating from approximately 4000 to 2500 BC are rare, but all known examples contain specific alloys of iron and nickel that occur only in extraterrestrial objects, not on earth. It took thousands of years of technological advances before civilizations developed iron [[term:smelting|term-00014]], the ability to extract a pure element from its naturally occurring ores and for iron tools to become common.","is":"Forfeðrum okkar var kunnugt um járn, kopar, silfur og gull. Tímabil í mannkynssögunni sem kallast bronsöld og járnöld marka þær framfarir þegar samfélög lærðu að einangra ákveðna málma og nota þá til að búa til verkfæri og vörur. Náttúrulegar málmgrýtisæðar af kopar, silfri og gulli geta innihaldið háan styrk þessara málma á frumefnisformi ([[xref:CNX_Chem_19_01_CuFeAu]]). Járn kemur hins vegar nánast eingöngu fyrir á jörðinni á oxuðu formi, svo sem ryð (Fe[[sub:2]]O[[sub:3]]). Fyrstu þekktu járngripirnir voru gerðir úr járnloftsteinum. Varðveittir járngripir frá því um 4000 til 2500 f.Kr. eru sjaldgæfir, en öll þekkt dæmi innihalda sérstakar málmblöndur af járni og nikkeli sem koma aðeins fyrir í geimfyrirbærum, ekki á jörðinni. Það tók þúsundir ára tækniframfara áður en samfélög þróuðu [[term:málmbræðslu|term-00014]] járns, hæfileikann til að vinna hreint frumefni úr náttúrulegum málmgrýtisæðum þess, og áður en járnverkfæri urðu algeng."},{"key":"m68842:caption:CNX_Chem_19_01_CuFeAu-caption","en":"Transition metals occur in nature in various forms. Examples include (a) a nugget of copper, (b) a deposit of gold, and (c) an ore containing oxidized iron. (credit a: modification of work by http://images-of-elements.com/copper-2.jpg; credit c: modification of work by http://images-of-elements.com/iron-ore.jpg)","is":"Hliðarfrumefni koma fyrir í náttúrunni á ýmsum formum. Dæmi eru (a) koparmoli, (b) gullnáma og (c) málmgrýti sem inniheldur oxað járn. (heimild a: breytt útgáfa af verki frá http://images-of-elements.com/copper-2.jpg; heimild c: breytt útgáfa af verki frá http://images-of-elements.com/iron-ore.jpg)"},{"key":"m68842:alt:fs-idm192179024-alt","en":"Three images are provided. In a, a smooth chunk of a copper-colored metal with an uneven surface is shown. In b, a dull gold chunk of a metal is shown. This chunk has a rough surface to which smaller chunks appear to be attached. In c, a rust colored chunk of a solid material with a dull surface is shown.","is":"Þrjár myndir eru sýndar. Á a) er sýndur sléttur moli af koparlituðum málmi með ójöfnu yfirborði. Á b) er sýndur daufgylltur málmmoli. Þessi moli hefur hrjúft yfirborð sem smærri molar virðast vera fastir við. Á c) er sýndur ryðlitaður moli af föstu efni með daufu yfirborði."},{"key":"m68842:para:fs-idm229647584","en":"Generally, the transition elements are extracted from minerals found in a variety of ores. However, the ease of their recovery varies widely, depending on the concentration of the element in the ore, the identity of the other elements present, and the difficulty of reducing the element to the free metal.","is":"Yfirleitt eru hliðarfrumefni unnin úr steinefnum sem finnast í ýmsum málmgrýtisæðum. Hins vegar er mjög misjafnt hversu auðvelt er að vinna þau, allt eftir styrk frumefnisins í málmgrýtinu, hvaða önnur frumefni eru til staðar og hversu erfitt er að afoxa frumefnið í hreinan málm."},{"key":"m68842:para:fs-idm221083280","en":"In general, it is not difficult to reduce ions of the [[i:d]]-block elements to the free element. Carbon is a sufficiently strong reducing agent in most cases. However, like the ions of the more active main group metals, ions of the [[i:f]]-block elements must be isolated by electrolysis or by reduction with an active metal such as calcium.","is":"Almennt er ekki erfitt að afoxa jónir [[i:d]]-blakkar frumefna í hreint frumefni. Kolefni er nægilega sterkt afoxunarefni í flestum tilfellum. Hins vegar, líkt og jónir virkari aðalflokksmálma, verður að einangra jónir [[i:f]]-blakkar frumefna með rafgreiningu eða með afoxun með virkum málmi eins og kalsíum."},{"key":"m68842:para:fs-idm203669440","en":"We shall discuss the processes used for the isolation of iron, copper, and silver because these three processes illustrate the principal means of isolating most of the [[i:d]]-block metals. In general, each of these processes involves three principal steps: preliminary treatment, smelting, and refining.","is":"Við munum ræða ferlana sem notaðir eru til að einangra járn, kopar og silfur því þessir þrír ferlar sýna helstu aðferðirnar til að einangra flesta [[i:d]]-blakkar málma. Almennt séð felur hver þessara ferla í sér þrjú meginþrep: forvinnslu, málmbræðslu og hreinsun."},{"key":"m68842:item:fs-idm273763504-item-1","en":"Preliminary treatment. In general, there is an initial treatment of the ores to make them suitable for the extraction of the metals. This usually involves crushing or grinding the ore, concentrating the metal-bearing components, and sometimes treating these substances chemically to convert them into compounds that are easier to reduce to the metal.","is":"Forvinnsla. Almennt er málmgrýtið forunnið til að gera það hæft til vinnslu málmanna. Þetta felur venjulega í sér að mylja eða mala málmgrýtið, auðga málmberandi hluti og stundum meðhöndla þessi efni efnafræðilega til að breyta þeim í efnasambönd sem auðveldara er að afoxa í málm."},{"key":"m68842:item:fs-idm273763504-item-2","en":"Smelting. The next step is the extraction of the metal in the molten state, a process called smelting, which includes reduction of the metallic compound to the metal. Impurities may be removed by the addition of a compound that forms a slag—a substance with a low melting point that can be readily separated from the molten metal.","is":"Málmbræðsla. Næsta skref er vinnsla málmsins á bráðnu formi, ferli sem kallast málmbræðsla, sem felur í sér afoxun málmsambandsins í málm. The final step in the recovery of a metal is refining the metal. Low boiling metals such as zinc and mercury can be refined by distillation. Þegar málmar með lágt bræðslumark, eins og tin, eru bræddir á hallandi borði, renna þeir frá óhreinindum með hærra bræðslumark. Coke is a form of carbon formed by heating coal in the absence of air to remove impurities.","is":"Snemmbúin notkun járns til framleiðslu á verkfærum og vopnum var möguleg vegna mikillar útbreiðslu járngrýtis og hversu auðvelt var að afoxa járnsambönd í málmgrýtinu með kolefni. Koks er form kolefnis sem myndast við hitun kola án lofts til að fjarlægja óhreinindi."},{"key":"m68842:para:fs-idm281682464","en":"The first step in the metallurgy of iron is usually roasting the ore (heating the ore in air) to remove water, decomposing carbonates into oxides, and converting sulfides into oxides. # Editing an Icelandic machine translation of a chemistry textbook (fable-editor, version 1)

You are editing the Icelandic machine translation of an English chemistry textbook (OpenStax _Chemistry 2e_),
which is being published as a free textbook for Icelandic upper-secondary students (aged about 16 to 20).
Work as an experienced Icelandic editor (yfirlesari) with a good knowledge of chemistry.

The goal is text a student can learn from: correct Icelandic in a register that is semi-academic but fluent
for younger readers. Judge grammar, agreement, word order and word choice in context, sentence by sentence and
across the passage. The translation must stay faithful to the English: do not add, drop or localize content
(units, examples and names stay as in the English), and do not explain more than the English does.

## What you receive

One JSON document (`"format": "fable-editor-user/1"`):

- `chapter` and `module`: where the text comes from.
- `englishContext`: the whole module in English, for context. Read it to understand the passage; edit only
  the `segments`.
- `terms`: the project's house terminology for this text. Each entry has the English forms (`en`) and the
  ruled Icelandic (`is`); `avoid` lists renderings known to be wrong for it. Use the ruled term, inflected as
  the sentence needs, wherever the English uses that term in that sense. Where no ruled term applies, choose
  the established Icelandic chemistry term.
- `segments`: in document order, each with a `key`, the English (`en`) and the machine translation (`is`).
  Segments are sentences, paragraphs, captions, list items, table cells or titles.

Both texts hold inline markers in double square brackets, such as `[[term:millikrafta|term-00001]]`,
`[[i:aq]]`, `[[sub:2]]`, `[[MATH:3]]`, `[[xref:CNX_Chem_10_01_KMTPhases1]]` or
`[[link:gagnvirku hermun|http://openstax.org/l/16phetvisual]]`. They carry formatting, formulas and
references. Keep every marker, with the same type and the same number of markers in the segment. You may edit
the Icelandic words inside a `term`, `link`, `i`, `b`, `em` or `u` marker, but never the part after `|`, and
never the contents of `MATH`, `MEDIA`, `TABLE`, `xref` or `docref` markers, or of `sub` and `sup` markers that
hold formula parts. You may move a marker within the segment when Icelandic word order needs it.

## What to return

Only the segments you change, each with its `key`, the whole edited Icelandic text of that segment, and one or
more tags saying what kind of change you made:

- `terminology`: a term changed to the house term or the established term;
- `grammar`: inflection, agreement, case, or another grammatical error;
- `fluency`: word order, phrasing or idiom, so the sentence reads as natural Icelandic;
- `meaning`: the translation said something the English does not;
- `register`: too formal, too colloquial, or too hard for the readers;
- `punctuation`: punctuation, capitals, spacing or number format.

Leave a segment out when it is already good. Each key appears at most once. Change only what improves the
text; a good machine-translated sentence does not need rewording.

{"format":"fable-editor-user/1","chapter":"ch19","module":"m68842","englishContext":"Occurrence, Preparation, and Properties of Transition Metals and Their Compounds

Transition metals are defined as those elements that have (or readily form) partially filled [[i:d]] orbitals. As shown in [[xref:CNX_Chem_19_01_PeriodicEConfig]], the [[term:[[i:d]]-block elements|term-00001]] in groups 3–11 are transition elements. The [[term:[[i:f]]-block elements|term-00002]], also called [[i:inner transition metals]] (the lanthanides and actinides), also meet this criterion because the [[i:d]] orbital is partially occupied before the [[i:f]] orbitals. The [[i:d]] orbitals fill with the copper family (group 11); for this reason, the next family (group 12) are technically not transition elements. However, the group 12 elements do display some of the same chemical properties and are commonly included in discussions of transition metals. Some chemists do treat the group 12 elements as transition metals.

The transition metals are located in groups 3–11 of the periodic table. The inner transition metals are in the two rows below the body of the table.

The Periodic Table of Elements is shown. The 18 columns are labeled “Group” and the 7 rows are labeled “Period.” Below the table to the right is a box labeled “Color Code” with different colors for metals, metalloids, and nonmetals, as well as solids, liquids, and gases. To the left of this box is an enlarged picture of the upper-left most box on the table. The number 1 is in its upper-left hand corner and is labeled “Atomic number.” The letter “H” is in the middle in red indicating that it is a gas. It is labeled “Symbol.” Below that is the number 1.008 which is labeled “Atomic Mass.” Below that is the word hydrogen which is labeled “name.” The color of the box indicates that it is a nonmetal. Beginning at the top left of the table, or period 1, group 1, is a box containing “1; hydrogen; H; nonmetal; gas; and 1.008.” There is only one other element box in period 1, group 18, which contains “2; The [[i:d]]-block elements are divided into the [[term:first transition series|term-00003]] (the elements Sc through Cu), the [[term:second transition series|term-00004]] (the elements Y through Ag), and the [[term:third transition series|term-00005]] (the element La and the elements Hf through Au). Actinium, Ac, is the first member of the [[term:fourth transition series|term-00006]], which also includes Rf through Rg.

The [[i:f]]-block elements are the elements Ce through Lu, which constitute the [[term:lanthanide series|term-00007]] (or [[term:lanthanoid series|term-00008]]), and the elements Th through Lr, which constitute the [[term:actinide series|term-00009]] (or [[term:actinoid series|term-00010]]). Because lanthanum behaves very much like the lanthanide elements, it is considered a lanthanide element, even though its electron configuration makes it the first member of the third transition series. Similarly, the behavior of actinium means it is part of the actinide series, although its electron configuration makes it the first member of the fourth transition series.

Uses of Lanthanides in Devices

Lanthanides (elements 57–71) are fairly abundant in the earth’s crust, despite their historic characterization as [[term:rare earth elements|term-00011]]. Thulium, the rarest naturally occurring lanthanoid, is more common in the earth’s crust than silver (4.5 [[MATH:1]] 10[[sup:−5]]% versus 0.79 [[MATH:2]] 10[[sup:−5]]% by mass). There are 17 rare earth elements, consisting of the 15 lanthanoids plus scandium and yttrium. They are called rare because they were once difficult to extract economically, so it was rare to have a pure sample; due to similar chemical properties, it is difficult to separate any one lanthanide from the others. However, newer separation methods, such as ion exchange resins similar to those found in home water softeners, make the separation of these elements easier and more economical. Most ores that contain these elements have low concentrations of all the rare earth elements mixed together.

The commercial applications of lanthanides are growing rapidly. For example, europium is important in flat screen displays found in computer monitors, cell phones, and televisions. Neodymium is useful in laptop hard drives and in the processes that convert crude oil into gasoline ([[xref:CNX_Chem_19_01_Lanthanoid]]). Holmium is found in dental and medical equipment. In addition, many alternative energy technologies rely heavily on lanthanoids. Neodymium and dysprosium are key components of hybrid vehicle engines and the magnets used in wind turbines.

As the demand for lanthanide materials has increased faster than supply, prices have also increased. In 2008, dysprosium cost $110/kg; by 2014, the price had increased to $470/kg. Increasing the supply of lanthanoid elements is one of the most significant challenges facing the industries that rely on the optical and magnetic properties of these materials.

The transition elements have many properties in common with other metals. They are almost all hard, high-melting solids that conduct heat and electricity well. They readily form alloys and lose electrons to form stable cations. In addition, transition metals form a wide variety of stable [[term:coordination compounds|term-00012]], in which the central metal atom or ion acts as a Lewis acid and accepts one or more pairs of electrons. Many different molecules and ions can donate lone pairs to the metal center, serving as Lewis bases. In this chapter, we shall focus primarily on the chemical behavior of the elements of the first transition series.

Properties of the Transition Elements

Transition metals demonstrate a wide range of chemical behaviors. As can be seen from their reduction potentials (see [[docref:Appendix H|m68866]]), some transition metals are strong reducing agents, whereas others have very low reactivity. For example, the lanthanides all form stable 3+ aqueous cations. The driving force for such oxidations is similar to that of alkaline earth metals such as Be or Mg, forming Be[[sup:2+]] and Mg[[sup:2+]]. On the other hand, materials like platinum and gold have much higher reduction potentials. Their ability to resist oxidation makes them useful materials for constructing circuits and jewelry.

Ions of the lighter [[i:d]]-block elements, such as Cr[[sup:3+]], Fe[[sup:3+]], and Co[[sup:2+]], form colorful hydrated ions that are stable in water. However, ions in the period just below these (Mo[[sup:3+]], Ru[[sup:3+]], and Ir[[sup:2+]]) are unstable and react readily with oxygen from the air. The majority of simple, water-stable ions formed by the heavier [[i:d]]-block elements are oxyanions such as [[MATH:3]] and [[MATH:4]]

Ruthenium, osmium, rhodium, iridium, palladium, and platinum are the [[term:platinum metals|term-00013]]. With difficulty, they form simple cations that are stable in water, and, unlike the earlier elements in the second and third transition series, they do not form stable oxyanions.

Both the [[i:d]]- and [[i:f]]-block elements react with nonmetals to form binary compounds; heating is often required. These elements react with halogens to form a variety of halides ranging in oxidation state from 1+ to 6+. On heating, oxygen reacts with all of the transition elements except palladium, platinum, silver, and gold. The oxides of these latter metals can be formed using other reactants, but they decompose upon heating. The [[i:f]]-block elements, the elements of group 3, and the elements of the first transition series except copper react with aqueous solutions of acids, forming hydrogen gas and solutions of the corresponding salts.

Transition metals can form compounds with a wide range of oxidation states. Some of the observed oxidation states of the elements of the first transition series are shown in [[xref:CNX_Chem_19_01_Oxistatra]]. The values in the table are typical values; there are other known values, and it is possible to synthesize new additions. For the elements scandium through manganese (the first half of the first transition series), the highest oxidation state corresponds to the loss of all of the electrons in both the [[i:s]] and [[i:d]] orbitals of their valence shells. The titanium(IV) ion, for example, is formed when the titanium atom loses its two 3[[i:d]] and two 4[[i:s]] electrons. These highest oxidation states are the most stable forms of scandium, titanium, and vanadium. However, it is not possible to continue to remove all of the valence electrons from metals as we continue through the series. Iron is known to form oxidation states from 2+ to 6+, with iron(II) and iron(III) being the most common. Most of the elements of the first transition series form ions with a charge of 2+ or 3+ that are stable in water, although those of the early members of the series can be readily oxidized by air.

The elements of the second and third transition series generally are more stable in higher oxidation states than are the elements of the first series. In general, the atomic radius increases down a group, which leads to the ions of the second and third series being larger than are those in the first series. Removing electrons from orbitals that are located farther from the nucleus is easier than removing electrons close to the nucleus. For example, molybdenum and tungsten, members of group 6, are limited mostly to an oxidation state of 6+ in aqueous solution. Chromium, the lightest member of the group, forms stable Cr[[sup:3+]] ions in water and, in the absence of air, less stable Cr[[sup:2+]] ions. The sulfide with the highest oxidation state for chromium is Cr[[sub:2]]S[[sub:3]], which contains the Cr[[sup:3+]] ion. Molybdenum and tungsten form sulfides in which the metals exhibit oxidation states of 4+ and 6+.

Preparation of the Transition Elements

Ancient civilizations knew about iron, copper, silver, and gold. The time periods in human history known as the Bronze Age and Iron Age mark the advancements in which societies learned to isolate certain metals and use them to make tools and goods. Naturally occurring ores of copper, silver, and gold can contain high concentrations of these metals in elemental form ([[xref:CNX_Chem_19_01_CuFeAu]]). Iron, on the other hand, occurs on earth almost exclusively in oxidized forms, such as rust (Fe[[sub:2]]O[[sub:3]]). The earliest known iron implements were made from iron meteorites. Surviving iron artifacts dating from approximately 4000 to 2500 BC are rare, but all known examples contain specific alloys of iron and nickel that occur only in extraterrestrial objects, not on earth. It took thousands of years of technological advances before civilizations developed iron [[term:smelting|term-00014]], the ability to extract a pure element from its naturally occurring ores and for iron tools to become common.

Transition metals occur in nature in various forms. Examples include (a) a nugget of copper, (b) a deposit of gold, and (c) an ore containing oxidized iron. Generally, the transition elements are extracted from minerals found in a variety of ores. However, the ease of their recovery varies widely, depending on the concentration of the element in the ore, the identity of the other elements present, and the difficulty of reducing the element to the free metal.

In general, it is not difficult to reduce ions of the [[i:d]]-block elements to the free element. Carbon is a sufficiently strong reducing agent in most cases. However, like the ions of the more active main group metals, ions of the [[i:f]]-block elements must be isolated by electrolysis or by reduction with an active metal such as calcium.

We shall discuss the processes used for the isolation of iron, copper, and silver because these three processes illustrate the principal means of isolating most of the [[i:d]]-block metals. In general, each of these processes involves three principal steps: preliminary treatment, smelting, and refining.

Preliminary treatment. In general, there is an initial treatment of the ores to make them suitable for the extraction of the metals. This usually involves crushing or grinding the ore, concentrating the metal-bearing components, and sometimes treating these substances chemically to convert them into compounds that are easier to reduce to the metal.

Smelting. The next step is the extraction of the metal in the molten state, a process called smelting, which includes reduction of the metallic compound to the metal. Impurities may be removed by the addition of a compound that forms a slag—a substance with a low melting point that can be readily separated from the molten metal.

Refining. The final step in the recovery of a metal is refining the metal. Low boiling metals such as zinc and mercury can be refined by distillation. When fused on an inclined table, low melting metals like tin flow away from higher-melting impurities. Electrolysis is another common method for refining metals.

Isolation of Iron

The early application of iron to the manufacture of tools and weapons was possible because of the wide distribution of iron ores and the ease with which iron compounds in the ores could be reduced by carbon. For a long time, charcoal was the form of carbon used in the reduction process. The production and use of iron became much more widespread about 1620, when coke was introduced as the reducing agent. Coke is a form of carbon formed by heating coal in the absence of air to remove impurities.

The first step in the metallurgy of iron is usually roasting the ore (heating the ore in air) to remove water, decomposing carbonates into oxides, and converting sulfides into oxides. The oxides are then reduced in a blast furnace that is 80–100 feet high and about 25 feet in diameter ([[xref:CNX_Chem_19_01_BlastFurn]]) in which the roasted ore, coke, and limestone (impure CaCO[[sub:3]]) are introduced continuously into the top. Molten iron and slag are withdrawn at the bottom. The entire stock in a furnace may weigh several hundred tons.

Within a blast furnace, different reactions occur in different temperature zones. Carbon monoxide is generated in the hotter bottom regions and rises upward to reduce the iron oxides to pure iron through a series of reactions that take place in the upper regions.

Much of the iron produced is refined and converted into steel. [[term:Steel|term-00015]] is made from iron by removing impurities and adding substances such as manganese, chromium, nickel, tungsten, molybdenum, and vanadium to produce alloys with properties that make the material suitable for specific uses. Most steels also contain small but definite percentages of carbon (0.04%–2.5%). However, a large part of the carbon contained in iron must be removed in the manufacture of steel; otherwise, the excess carbon would make the iron brittle.

Isolation of Copper

The most important ores of copper contain copper sulfides (such as covellite, CuS), although copper oxides (such as tenorite, CuO) and copper hydroxycarbonates [such as malachite, Cu[[sub:2]](OH)[[sub:2]]CO[[sub:3]]] are sometimes found. In the production of copper metal, the concentrated sulfide ore is roasted to remove part of the sulfur as sulfur dioxide. The remaining mixture, which consists of Cu[[sub:2]]S, FeS, FeO, and SiO[[sub:2]], is mixed with limestone, which serves as a flux (a material that aids in the removal of impurities), and heated. Molten slag forms as the iron and silica are removed by Lewis acid-base reactions:

In these reactions, the silicon dioxide behaves as a Lewis acid, which accepts a pair of electrons from the Lewis base (the oxide ion).

Silver sometimes occurs in large nuggets ([[xref:CNX_Chem_19_01_Ag]]) but more frequently in veins and related deposits.
